stem:
Complete the following statement to show how the production process in the garment industry is spread across countries.

‘The brand tag says “Made in Thailand” but they are not Thai products. We dissect the manufacturing process and look for the best solution at each step. We are doing it globally. In making garments, the company may, for example, get cotton fibre from Korea, ........’
solution:
A possible completion:

‘… get cotton fibre from Korea, have it spun into yarn and woven into fabric in China, get the fabric dyed and printed in Bangladesh, buy the buttons and zips from Japan, have the garments stitched in Thailand, and sell the finished garments in the markets of Europe and North America under its own brand name.’

Each step is placed where it can be done best and cheapest. The production process is therefore divided into small parts and spread out across the globe, and the finished garment carries a single ‘Made in Thailand’ tag although several countries have contributed to it.
groundedIn: § Production Across Countries — MNCs setting up offices and factories for production in regions where they can get cheap labour and other resources so that the cost of production is low; § Spreading of Production — the chapter's worked example of one MNC designing its products in the United States, having the components manufactured in China, assembling them in Mexico and Eastern Europe and running customer care from India

context:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Ford Motors, an American company, is one of the world's largest automobile manufacturers with production spread over 26 countries of the world. Ford Motors came to India in 1995 and spent Rs. 1700 crore to set up a large plant near Chennai. This was done in collaboration with Mahindra and Mahindra, a major Indian manufacturer of jeeps and trucks. By the year 2017, Ford Motors was selling 88,000 cars in the Indian markets, while another 1,81,000 cars were exported from India to South Africa, Mexico, Brazil and United States of America. The company wants to develop Ford India as a component supplying base for its other plants across the globe.
stem: Would you say Ford Motors is a MNC? Why?
solution:
**Yes, Ford Motors is a MNC.**

1. A MNC is a company that **owns or controls production in more than one nation**.
2. Ford Motors is an American company whose production is spread over **26 countries** of the world.
3. It owns and runs a large plant near Chennai in India, set up in 1995 in collaboration with Mahindra and Mahindra.
groundedIn: § Production Across Countries — the chapter's definition of a MNC as a company that owns or controls production in more than one nation

stem: What is foreign investment? How much did Ford Motors invest in India?
solution:
**Foreign investment is investment made by a MNC.**

1. The money that is spent to buy assets such as land, building, machines and other equipment is called **investment**, and investment made by MNCs is called **foreign investment**.
2. Any such investment is made with the hope that these assets will earn profits.
3. Ford Motors spent **Rs 1700 crore** to set up its large plant near Chennai in 1995.
groundedIn: § Interlinking Production Across — the chapter's definition of investment as the money spent to buy assets such as land, building, machines and other equipment, and of foreign investment as investment made by MNCs

This was done in collaboration with Mahindra and Mahindra, a major Indian manufacturer of jeeps and trucks. By the year 2017, Ford Motors was selling 88,000 cars in the Indian markets, while another 1,81,000 cars were exported from India to South Africa, Mexico, Brazil and United States of America. The company wants to develop Ford India as a component supplying base for its other plants across the globe.
stem: By setting up their production plants in India, MNCs such as Ford Motors tap the advantage not only of the large markets that countries such as India provide, but also the lower costs of production. Explain the statement.
solution:
**Ford gains twice over in India — from the size of the market and from the cheapness of production.**

1. **Large market.** India is itself a very large market for cars; by 2017 Ford was selling 88,000 cars within India, and the plant is also close to the large number of buyers in India and China.
2. **Low cost of production.** MNCs set up production where skilled and unskilled labour is available at low costs and other factors of production are assured, so the cost of production is low and profits are greater.
3. **Local supply base.** Several local manufacturers supply auto-parts to Ford in India, which lowers its component costs further.
4. Because costs are low, cars made in India can also be **exported** — 1,81,000 were sent to South Africa, Mexico, Brazil and the USA — and India can serve as a component supplying base for Ford's other plants.
groundedIn: § Production Across Countries — MNCs setting up offices and factories for production in regions where they can get cheap labour and other resources so that the cost of production is low and greater profits can be earned; § Interlinking Production Across — MNCs setting up production where it is close to the markets and where skilled and unskilled labour is available at low costs

stem:
Why do you think the company wants to develop India as a base for manufacturing car components for its global operations? Discuss the following factors:

(a) cost of labour and other resources in India
(b) the presence of several local manufacturers who supply auto-parts to Ford Motors
(c) closeness to a large number of buyers in India and China
solution:
**India is a cheap and well-supplied place from which Ford can send components to its plants everywhere.**

1. **(a) Cost of labour and other resources.** Skilled and unskilled labour is available in India at low cost and other factors of production are assured, so components made here cost Ford far less than components made in the United States or Europe.
2. **(b) Presence of local auto-parts manufacturers.** A ready base of local suppliers means Ford need not make every part itself; it can buy from local companies, and those companies in turn raise their own production standards.
3. **(c) Closeness to buyers in India and China.** The plant sits near two very large markets, so finished cars and components reach buyers quickly and transport costs are saved.

Together these make India a low-cost component supplying base for Ford's other plants across the globe.
groundedIn: § Interlinking Production Across — MNCs setting up production where it is close to the markets, where there is skilled and unskilled labour available at low costs, and where the availability of other factors of production is assured; § Production Across Countries — MNCs setting up production where they can get cheap labour and other resources so that the cost of production is low

This was done in collaboration with Mahindra and Mahindra, a major Indian manufacturer of jeeps and trucks. By the year 2017, Ford Motors was selling 88,000 cars in the Indian markets, while another 1,81,000 cars were exported from India to South Africa, Mexico, Brazil and United States of America. The company wants to develop Ford India as a component supplying base for its other plants across the globe.
stem: In what ways will the production of cars by Ford Motors in India lead to interlinking of production?
solution:
**Ford's Indian plant ties production in India to production in many other countries.**

1. Ford produces cars in India **jointly with Mahindra and Mahindra**, an Indian company, so the production of the two companies is linked.
2. It buys auto-parts from **local Indian manufacturers**, which brings small and medium Indian producers into Ford's global production chain.
3. Cars made in India are **exported** to South Africa, Mexico, Brazil and the United States, linking Indian production with markets abroad.
4. India is being developed as a **component supplying base** for Ford's other plants, so components made here go into cars assembled in other countries.

In this way production in widely dispersed locations gets interlinked.
groundedIn: § Interlinking Production Across — MNCs setting up production jointly with local companies, using the local companies for supplies, and production in widely dispersed locations thereby getting interlinked

stem: In what ways is a MNC different from other companies?
solution:
| MNC | Other (domestic) company |
|---|---|
| Owns or controls production in more than one nation. | Owns and runs production within one country only. |
| Sets up offices and factories abroad, in regions where labour and other resources are cheap. | Produces where it is; it cannot move to a cheaper country. |
| Its goods and services are produced globally — the production process is divided into small parts spread across the globe. | The whole production process is carried out within the country. |
| Makes foreign investment — buys land, buildings and machines in other countries. | Invests within its own country. |
| Many top MNCs have wealth exceeding the entire budgets of developing country governments, and can determine price, quality, delivery and labour conditions for distant producers. | Has no such wealth, and no such power over producers in other countries. |
groundedIn: § Production Across Countries — the definition of a MNC as a company that owns or controls production in more than one nation and sets up offices and factories where labour and other resources are cheap; § Interlinking Production Across — top MNCs having wealth exceeding the entire budgets of developing country governments and determining price, quality, delivery and labour conditions for distant producers

stem: Nearly all major multinationals are American, Japanese or European, such as Nike, Coca-Cola, Pepsi, Honda, Nokia. Can you guess why?
solution:
**Because these are the developed countries, where the wealth and the technology needed to spread production across the world are concentrated.** (This is one defensible answer among several.)

1. Their companies have **enormous wealth** — many of the top MNCs have wealth exceeding the entire budgets of developing country governments — so they can buy up companies abroad and invest in new plants.
2. They command the **latest technology** for production, which they can carry with them into the countries where they invest.
3. Their home countries are **rich markets**, so they can sell profitably at home while shifting production to cheaper locations abroad.
4. Rapid improvements in transport and in information and communication technology let them **divide production across the globe** and still control it from their own countries.
groundedIn: § Interlinking Production Across — many of the top MNCs having wealth exceeding the entire budgets of developing country governments, and MNCs bringing the latest technology for production; § Factors that Have Enabled Globalisation — rapid improvement in transportation technology and in information and communication technology

subtopic: Foreign Trade and Integration of Markets
stem: What was the main channel connecting countries in the past? How is it different now?
solution:
**In the past the main channel connecting countries was foreign trade.**

1. Until the middle of the twentieth century production was largely organised within countries; what crossed the boundaries were raw material, food stuff and finished products. Colonies such as India exported raw materials and food stuff and imported finished goods.
2. **Today countries are connected in many more ways.** Besides trade there is foreign investment by MNCs, movement of technology, and services produced in one country for buyers in another; people also move between countries, though not much more than before.
3. **Production itself now crosses borders.** MNCs divide the production process into small parts spread across the globe, so goods and services are produced globally and not merely sold globally.
groundedIn: § Production Across Countries — production being largely organised within countries until the middle of the twentieth century, with trade the main channel connecting distant countries; § What is Globalisation — goods, services, investments and technology moving between countries today, and the movement of people as one more way in which countries can be connected

subtopic: Foreign Trade and Integration of Markets
stem: Distinguish between foreign trade and foreign investment.
solution:
| Foreign trade | Foreign investment |
|---|---|
| Buying and selling of goods and services across countries, that is, export and import. | Money spent by a MNC to buy assets such as land, building, machines and other equipment in another country. |
| Only the goods cross the border; production stays where it was. | Production itself is set up in the other country. |
| It lets producers reach beyond their domestic markets and lets buyers expand their choice of goods. | It is made with the hope that these assets will earn profits for the MNC. |
| Example: Chinese toys sold in the Indian markets. | Example: Ford Motors spending Rs 1700 crore on a plant near Chennai. |
groundedIn: § Foreign Trade and Integration of — foreign trade creating an opportunity for producers to reach beyond the domestic markets and for buyers to expand their choice of goods; § Interlinking Production Across — investment as the money spent to buy assets such as land, building, machines and other equipment, and foreign investment as investment made by MNCs

subtopic: Foreign Trade and Integration of Markets
stem:
In recent years China has been importing steel from India. Explain how the import of steel by China will affect.

(a) steel companies in China.
(b) steel companies in India.
(c) industries buying steel for production of other industrial goods in China.
solution:
| Affected group | Effect |
|---|---|
| **(a) Steel companies in China** | They face competition from Indian steel. Buyers now have a choice, prices are pushed down and their sales fall, so they face losses unless they cut costs or improve quality. |
| **(b) Steel companies in India** | They reach beyond the domestic market. Their sales and production expand and the export orders give them an opportunity to grow. |
| **(c) Chinese industries buying steel** | They gain. Steel is available at a lower price and with greater choice, so their cost of production falls and they can sell their own goods cheaper. |

This is the same pattern as Chinese toys in India: with the opening of trade the exporting country's producers expand business, the buyers gain, and the competing producers of the importing country face losses.
groundedIn: § Chinese Toys in India — the chapter's worked example in which the importing country's buyers get a greater choice at lower prices, the exporting country's producers get an opportunity to expand business and the competing domestic producers face losses; § Foreign Trade and Integration of — foreign trade letting producers reach beyond the domestic markets and letting buyers expand their choice of goods

subtopic: Foreign Trade and Integration of Markets
stem: How will the import of steel from India into the Chinese markets lead to integration of markets for steel in the two countries? Explain.
solution:
**Once steel moves between them, the Indian and Chinese steel markets begin to behave as one market.**

1. Steel travels from the Indian market into the Chinese market, so the **choice of steel rises** for Chinese buyers.
2. **Prices of steel in the two markets tend to become equal**, because no buyer will pay much more in one market than in the other.
3. Steel producers in India and in China now **closely compete against each other**, even though they are separated by thousands of miles.
4. Foreign trade thus results in connecting the markets, that is, integration of the markets of the two countries.
groundedIn: § Integration of Markets in Different — the chapter's statement that foreign trade results in connecting the markets, or integration of markets, in different countries; § Foreign Trade and Integration of — with the opening of trade goods travelling from one market to another, choice of goods rising, prices of similar goods tending to become equal and producers closely competing

stem: What is the role of MNCs in the globalisation process?
solution:
**MNCs are the main force driving the globalisation process.**

1. They **spread production across countries**, placing each part of the production process where it is cheapest or best, so production is organised in increasingly complex ways.
2. They make **foreign investment** — setting up factories and offices, buying up local companies, or producing jointly with local companies.
3. They **control a large part of foreign trade**: Ford Motors in India exports cars to other developing countries and car components to its factories around the world.
4. They carry **money and the latest technology** into the countries where they invest.
5. By all this, production in widely dispersed locations gets **interlinked** and markets across countries get integrated.
groundedIn: § What is Globalisation — MNCs playing a major role in the globalisation process, with a large part of foreign trade also controlled by MNCs and the Ford plant exporting cars and components; § Interlinking Production Across — MNCs providing money for additional investments and bringing the latest technology, so that production in widely dispersed locations gets interlinked

stem: What are the various ways in which countries can be linked?
solution:
Countries can be linked in **five** ways:

1. **Foreign trade** — movement of goods between countries through exports and imports.
2. **Services** — services such as call centres, data entry, accounting and designing produced in one country for buyers in another.
3. **Foreign investment** — MNCs setting up or buying production in other countries.
4. **Technology** — movement of technology between countries, largely through MNCs.
5. **Movement of people** — people moving from one country to another in search of better income, better jobs or better education, though this has not increased much in the past few decades because of various restrictions.
groundedIn: § What is Globalisation — more and more goods and services, investments and technology moving between countries, and the movement of people as one more way in which countries can be connected, restricted in practice

stem:
Choose the correct option.

Globalisation, by connecting countries, shall result in

(a) lesser competition among producers.
(b) greater competition among producers.
(c) no change in competition among producers.
solution:
**(b) greater competition among producers.**

Once trade opens, producers in the two countries closely compete against each other even though they are separated by thousands of miles. It is this greater competition among producers, both local and foreign, that gives consumers greater choice, improved quality and lower prices.
groundedIn: § Foreign Trade and Integration of — producers in the two countries closely competing against each other once trade opens; § Impact of Globalisation in India — globalisation and greater competition among producers, both local and foreign, being of advantage to consumers

context:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Information and communication technology (or IT in short) has played a major role in spreading out production of services across countries. Let us see how.

A news magazine published for London readers is to be designed and printed in Delhi. The text of the magazine is sent through Internet to the Delhi office. The designers in the Delhi office get orders on how to design the magazine from the office in London using telecommunication facilities. The designing is done on a computer. After printing, the magazines are sent by air to London. Even the payment of money for designing and printing from a bank in London to a bank in Delhi is done instantly through the Internet (e-banking)!
stem: In the above example, underline the words describing the use of technology in production.
solution:
The words describing the use of technology are:

1. **sent through Internet** — the text of the magazine reaches the Delhi office.
2. **using telecommunication facilities** — the London office gives the designers their orders.
3. **done on a computer** — the designing itself.
4. **printing** — the magazine is printed in Delhi.
5. **sent by air** — improved transport carries the magazines to London.
6. **instantly through the Internet (e-banking)** — the payment is made.

Every one of these is a use of information and communication technology or of improved transport, and together they let a service be produced in Delhi for buyers in London.
groundedIn: § Using IT in — the chapter's worked example of a London magazine designed and printed in Delhi through the Internet, telecommunication facilities, a computer, air transport and e-banking; § Factors that Have Enabled Globalisation — rapid improvement in transportation technology and the developments in information and communication technology

stem: How is information technology connected with globalisation? Would globalisation have been possible without expansion of IT?
solution:
**Information technology is what has made the spreading out of production of services across countries possible.**

1. **Telecommunication facilities** — telegraph, telephone including mobile phones, fax — are used to contact one another around the world, to access information instantly and to communicate from remote areas, facilitated by satellite communication devices.
2. **Computers** have now entered almost every field of activity, and the **Internet** allows information to be obtained and shared on almost anything.
3. The Internet allows instant e-mail and voice-mail across the world at **negligible costs**, and payment can be made instantly through e-banking.
4. Because of this, services such as designing, data entry, accounting, administrative tasks and engineering can be produced in India and delivered in London or New York.

**No, globalisation on the present scale would not have been possible without the expansion of IT.** Without instant and cheap communication a MNC could not divide its production process across several countries or control it from a distance, and call centres and service exports could not exist at all. Trade in goods would still have been possible, but production and markets could not have been integrated in the way they are today.
groundedIn: § Factors that Have Enabled Globalisation — the developments in telecommunications, computers and the Internet, and instant e-mail and voice-mail across the world at negligible costs; § Using IT in — information and communication technology having played a major role in spreading out production of services across countries

stem: What do you understand by liberalisation of foreign trade?
solution:
**Liberalisation of foreign trade means removing the barriers or restrictions on trade that the government had set up.**

1. Barriers such as a **tax on imports**, or a limit on the quantity that may be imported, are removed, so goods can be imported and exported easily.
2. Businesses are allowed to **make decisions freely** about what they wish to import or export.
3. The government imposes much less restriction than before and is therefore said to be more **liberal**.
4. In India these barriers were removed to a large extent starting around **1991**, so that Indian producers would compete with producers around the globe and improve their quality.
groundedIn: § Removing Barriers or Restrictions — the chapter's definition of liberalisation as removing barriers or restrictions set by the government, with businesses then free to decide what to import or export; § Liberalisation of Foreign Trade — the far-reaching policy changes made in India starting around 1991, after which goods could be imported and exported easily

stem: Tax on imports is one type of trade barrier. The government could also place a limit on the number of goods that can be imported. This is known as quotas. Can you explain, using the example of Chinese toys, how quotas can be used as trade barriers? Do you think this should be used? Discuss.
solution:
**How a quota would work on Chinese toys:**

1. A quota fixes the **maximum number** of toys that may be imported from China in a year.
2. Once that limit is reached, no more Chinese toys can enter, so the supply of cheap Chinese toys in the Indian market is cut short.
3. Buyers who still want toys must buy **Indian toys**, so Indian toy-makers keep their sales instead of being replaced in 70 to 80 per cent of the shops.
4. With supply restricted, the price of Chinese toys in India rises and the cheapness that made them popular disappears.

A quota is therefore a trade barrier, exactly like a tax on imports, because it is a restriction that lets the government decide what kinds of goods and how much of each should come into the country.

**Should it be used?** Yes, but only for a limited period and for an industry that is just coming up, as India protected its new industries in the 1950s and 1960s. Used permanently a quota removes the pressure on producers to improve quality, and the consumer pays a higher price for a poorer toy. (This is one defensible answer among several.)
groundedIn: § Chinese Toys in India — the chapter's example in which cheaper Chinese toys replaced Indian toys in 70 to 80 per cent of the toy shops and Indian toy makers faced losses; § Liberalisation of Foreign Trade — tax on imports as an example of a trade barrier, governments using trade barriers to regulate foreign trade and to decide what goods should come into the country, and the protection given to Indian industries coming up in the 1950s and 1960s

stem:
Fill in the blanks.

WTO was started at the initiative of __________ countries. The aim of the WTO is to ____________________. WTO establishes rules regarding ________________ for all countries, and sees that ___________________. In practice, trade between countries is not ______________________________. Developing countries like India have ___________________, whereas developed countries, in many cases, have continued to provide protection to their producers.
solution:
1. **developed**
2. **liberalise international trade**
3. **international trade**
4. **these rules are obeyed**
5. **free and fair**
6. **removed their trade barriers as per WTO rules**

The completed passage reads: WTO was started at the initiative of **developed** countries. The aim of the WTO is to **liberalise international trade**. WTO establishes rules regarding **international trade** for all countries, and sees that **these rules are obeyed**. In practice, trade between countries is not **free and fair**. Developing countries like India have **removed their trade barriers as per WTO rules**, whereas developed countries, in many cases, have continued to provide protection to their producers.
groundedIn: § World Trade Organisation — the WTO being started at the initiative of the developed countries, its aim of liberalising international trade, its establishing rules regarding international trade and seeing that these rules are obeyed, and the developed countries unfairly retaining trade barriers while WTO rules forced the developing countries to remove theirs

stem: What do you think can be done so that trade between countries is more fair?
solution:
**Trade would be fairer if the rules applied equally to developed and developing countries.** Steps that can be taken:

1. Developed countries must **remove the trade barriers they have unfairly retained**, as the developing countries have already done under WTO rules.
2. They must **stop paying their farmers vast sums of money** for production and export, which lets surplus farm products be sold in other country markets at abnormally low prices and hurts farmers there.
3. Developing countries should **negotiate at the WTO for ‘fairer rules’**.
4. They should **align with other developing countries** having similar interests, to fight the domination of the developed countries in the WTO.
5. Governments may **use trade and investment barriers** where necessary, and support small producers until they are strong enough to compete.
6. **People's organisations** can campaign and make representations; such campaigns have already influenced important decisions relating to trade and investment at the WTO.
groundedIn: § Debate on Trade Practices — the developing countries asking the developed country governments why they continue to pay their farmers vast sums of money while asking others to stop supporting theirs; § World Trade Organisation — developed countries unfairly retaining trade barriers while WTO rules forced developing countries to remove theirs; § The Struggle for a Fair Globalisation — the government negotiating at the WTO for ‘fairer rules’, aligning with other developing countries, and campaigns by people's organisations influencing decisions at the WTO

stem: In the above example, we saw that the US government gives massive sums of money to farmers for production. At times, governments also give support to promote production of certain types of goods, such as those which are environmentally friendly. Discuss whether these are fair or not.
solution:
**Support that changes what is produced at home is fair; support that lets surplus produce be dumped in another country's market at abnormally low prices is not.** (This is one defensible answer among several.)

1. The test is **whom the support harms**. In the US the support goes to a tiny 0.5 per cent of the workforce, and because of it US farmers can sell farm products at abnormally low prices, the surplus being sold in other country markets and adversely affecting farmers there.
2. Support for environmentally friendly goods, by contrast, is meant to change **what** is produced rather than to capture another country's market. It makes a socially useful product cheaper without pushing foreign producers out of their own market.
3. It becomes unfair the moment it turns into an export subsidy that undercuts producers abroad, or when only rich countries can afford it while WTO rules deny poorer countries the same help.
4. Such support should therefore be allowed only where it is open, limited in amount and **not tied to exports** — and the same rule must bind developed and developing countries alike.
groundedIn: § Debate on Trade Practices — US farmers receiving massive sums of money from their government and selling surplus farm products in other country markets at low prices, adversely affecting farmers in those countries; § World Trade Organisation — the developed countries unfairly retaining trade barriers while WTO rules forced the developing countries to remove theirs

stem: How has competition benefited people in India?
solution:
**Greater competition among producers, both local and foreign, has been of advantage to consumers.**

1. There is **greater choice** of goods before consumers, particularly the well-off sections in the urban areas.
2. They enjoy **improved quality and lower prices** for several products.
3. As a result these people today enjoy much **higher standards of living** than was possible earlier.
4. **New jobs** have been created in the industries and services where MNCs have invested — cell phones, automobiles, electronics, soft drinks, fast food and banking — and local companies supplying raw materials to them have prospered.
5. Top Indian companies have **invested in newer technology and production methods and raised their production standards** in order to meet the competition.
groundedIn: § Impact of Globalisation in India — greater competition benefiting consumers with greater choice, improved quality, lower prices and higher standards of living, MNC investment creating new jobs and local supplying companies prospering, and top Indian companies raising their production standards

stem: Should more Indian companies emerge as MNCs? How would it benefit the people in the country?
solution:
**Yes, more Indian companies should emerge as MNCs.** (This is one defensible answer among several.)

1. Globalisation has already enabled some large Indian companies to become multinationals — **Tata Motors, Infosys, Ranbaxy, Asian Paints and Sundaram Fasteners** — and some Indian companies are spreading their operations worldwide.
2. A company that produces and sells in many countries earns **larger profits**, and part of that income returns to India.
3. To compete abroad such a company must **invest in newer technology and production methods and raise its production standards**, which improves the goods available to Indian buyers as well.
4. It creates **more jobs** at home, and the local companies that supply it with raw materials and components prosper.
5. It gives India a share of the gains from globalisation instead of leaving those gains to foreign MNCs alone.
groundedIn: § Impact of Globalisation in India — globalisation enabling some large Indian companies to emerge as multinationals themselves, such as Tata Motors, Infosys, Ranbaxy, Asian Paints and Sundaram Fasteners, and top Indian companies investing in newer technology and raising their production standards

stem: Why do governments try to attract more foreign investment?
solution:
**Because foreign investment brings money, technology and jobs that the country needs.**

1. MNCs bring **money for investment** in land, buildings and machines, and often the **latest technology** for production.
2. Their factories and offices create **new jobs**, and local companies supplying them with raw materials and components prosper.
3. Competing with them **raises the standards** of local producers, who must improve technology and quality.
4. That is why the central and state governments in India set up **Special Economic Zones (SEZs)** with world class facilities — electricity, water, roads, transport, storage, recreational and educational facilities — and exempt companies there from taxes for an initial period of five years.
5. The government has also allowed **flexibility in the labour laws** in order to attract foreign investment.
groundedIn: § Steps to Attract Foreign Investment — the special steps taken by the central and state governments, the SEZs with world class facilities, the five-year tax exemption and the flexibility allowed in the labour laws; § Interlinking Production Across — MNCs providing money for additional investments and bringing the latest technology for production

context:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Ravi did not expect that he would have to face a crisis in such a short period of his life as industrialist. Ravi took a loan from the bank to start his own company producing capacitors in 1992 in Hosur, an industrial town in Tamil Nadu. Capacitors are used in many electronic home appliances including tube lights, television etc. Within three years, he was able to expand production and had 20 workers working under him. His struggle to run his company started when the government removed restrictions on imports of capacitors as per its agreement at WTO in 2001. His main clients, the television companies, used to buy different components including capacitors in bulk for the manufacture of television sets. However, competition from the MNC brands forced the Indian television companies to move into assembling activities for MNCs. Even when some of them bought capacitors, they would prefer to import as the price of the imported item was half the price charged by people like Ravi. Ravi now produces less than half the capacitors that he produced in the year 2000 and has only seven workers working for him. Many of Ravi's friends in the same business in Hyderabad and Chennai have closed their units.
stem: What are the ways in which Ravi's small production unit was affected by rising competition?
solution:
**Ravi's unit was affected in four ways.**

1. **Loss of protection.** In 2001 the government removed restrictions on the import of capacitors as per its agreement at the WTO, so cheap imported capacitors entered the Indian market.
2. **Loss of clients.** Competition from the MNC brands forced his main clients, the Indian television companies, to move into assembling activities for MNCs, so they no longer bought components in bulk.
3. **Price disadvantage.** Even those who still bought capacitors preferred to import, because the price of the imported item was **half** the price he charged.
4. **Fall in production and employment.** He now produces **less than half** the capacitors he produced in 2000, and his workforce has fallen from **20 workers to seven**. Many of his friends in the same business in Hyderabad and Chennai have closed their units altogether.
groundedIn: § Rising Competition — the chapter's account of Ravi's capacitor unit after import restrictions were removed in 2001; § Small Producers Compete or Perish — small manufacturers in industries such as capacitors being hit hard by competition, with several units shutting down and rendering workers jobless

stem: Should producers such as Ravi stop production because their cost of production is higher compared to producers in other countries? What do you think?
solution:
**No, producers such as Ravi should not have to stop production.** (This is one defensible answer among several.)

1. His higher cost is not of his own making. Small producers in India lack **better roads, power, water, raw materials, marketing and information networks**, modern technology, and timely credit at reasonable interest rates; given these his cost would fall.
2. Small and medium industries in India employ the **largest number of workers (11 crores)** in the country, next only to agriculture, so closing them throws very large numbers out of work — Ravi's own workforce fell from 20 to seven.
3. The government can **support small producers to improve their performance** till the time they become strong enough to compete, and can use trade and investment barriers if necessary.
4. A globalisation that destroys the livelihood of the many while benefiting the well-off few is not fair globalisation; the benefits should be shared better.
groundedIn: § Small Producers Compete or Perish — small and medium industries in India employing the largest number of workers (11 crores) in the country, next only to agriculture, and several units shutting down; § The Struggle for a Fair Globalisation — the government supporting small producers to improve their performance till they become strong enough to compete, and using trade and investment barriers if necessary

stem:
Recent studies point out that small producers in India need three things to compete better in the market: (a) better roads, power, water, raw materials, marketing and information network (b) improvements and modernisation of technology (c) timely availability of credit at reasonable interest rates.

- Can you explain how these three things would help Indian producers?
- Do you think MNCs will be interested in investing in these? Why?
- Do you think the government has a role in making these facilities available? Why?
- Can you think of any other step that the government could take? Discuss.
solution:
**How the three things would help Indian producers**

1. **(a) Better roads, power, water, raw materials, marketing and information network.** Assured power and good roads cut production and transport costs and prevent losses from breakdowns; a marketing and information network tells a small producer where the demand and the better prices are.
2. **(b) Improvements and modernisation of technology.** Better machines raise output per worker and improve quality, so the producer can match the price and the standard of imported goods — the very thing Ravi could not do.
3. **(c) Timely credit at reasonable interest rates.** Cheap and timely loans let a small producer buy raw material in bulk and invest in new machines instead of borrowing at a high cost.

**Will MNCs be interested in investing in these?** Largely no. MNCs invest where there are a large number of well-off buyers and quick profits — cell phones, automobiles, electronics, soft drinks, fast food, banking. Roads, power and water are costly, slow to earn and benefit everyone alike, so MNCs expect these facilities to be **provided for them**, as they are inside the SEZs.

**Does the government have a role?** Yes. Its policies must protect the interests not only of the rich and the powerful but of all the people in the country. It already provides world class electricity, water, roads, transport and storage inside the SEZs, and these are exactly the facilities small producers need; it can also support small producers till they become strong enough to compete.

**Other steps the government could take:** ensure that labour laws are properly implemented so that workers get their rights; use trade and investment barriers where necessary; negotiate at the WTO for ‘fairer rules’; and align with other developing countries with similar interests. (These are defensible suggestions among several.)
groundedIn: § Small Producers Compete or Perish — the major challenges globalisation has posed for a large number of small producers and workers; § Steps to Attract Foreign Investment — the world class facilities of electricity, water, roads, transport and storage provided in the SEZs to attract foreign companies; § The Struggle for a Fair Globalisation — the government ensuring that labour laws are properly implemented, supporting small producers till they can compete, using trade and investment barriers and negotiating at the WTO for ‘fairer rules’

stem: In what ways has competition affected workers, Indian exporters and foreign MNCs in the garment industry?
solution:
| Group | Effect of competition |
|---|---|
| **Workers** | Their jobs are no longer secure. Permanent workers have given way to temporary workers hired only for short periods; wages are low, the benefits of a permanent worker — health insurance, provident fund and overtime at a double rate — are lost, and they must work very long hours and night shifts in the peak season. Sushila now earns less than half of what she earned earlier. |
| **Indian exporters** | They compete fiercely against one another for the large orders of the MNCs. As the cost of raw materials cannot be reduced, they try to cut **labour costs** — employing workers temporarily and paying low wages — so as to quote the cheapest price. |
| **Foreign MNCs** | They gain. With their worldwide networks they look for the cheapest goods, and the competition among the exporters lets them buy at low prices and make large profits. |

The workers are thus denied their fair share of the benefits brought about by globalisation.
groundedIn: § Competition and Uncertain Employment — employers preferring to employ workers ‘flexibly’ so that jobs are no longer secure, MNCs with worldwide networks looking for the cheapest goods, exporters cutting labour costs to win orders, and workers being denied their fair share of the benefits; § A Garment Worker — Sushila losing her permanent job and its benefits and earning less than half of what she earned earlier

subtopic: The Struggle for a Fair Globalisation
stem:
What can be done by each of the following so that the workers can get a fair share of benefits brought by globalisation?

(a) government
(b) employers at the exporting factories
(c) MNCs
(d) workers.
solution:
| Who | What can be done |
|---|---|
| **(a) Government** | Ensure that labour laws are properly implemented and that the workers get their rights; frame policies that protect the interests not only of the rich and the powerful but of all the people; support small producers till they are strong enough to compete; use trade and investment barriers if necessary; and negotiate at the WTO for ‘fairer rules’, aligning with other developing countries. |
| **(b) Employers at the exporting factories** | Employ workers on a permanent basis instead of ‘flexibly’; pay fair wages and the benefits due — health insurance, provident fund and overtime at a double rate; limit working hours and night shifts; and cut costs by raising productivity rather than by cutting labour costs. |
| **(c) MNCs** | Stop pressing only for the cheapest goods; pay the exporters a price that allows fair wages, and use the power they already have over price, quality, delivery and labour conditions to insist on decent conditions of work. |
| **(d) Workers** | Organise themselves and demand their rights and a fair share of the benefits. Massive campaigns and representation by people's organisations have already influenced important decisions relating to trade and investments at the WTO. |
groundedIn: § The Struggle for a Fair Globalisation — the government ensuring that labour laws are properly implemented so that workers get their rights, its policies protecting the interests of all the people, negotiation at the WTO for ‘fairer rules’, and campaigns by people's organisations influencing decisions at the WTO; § Competition and Uncertain Employment — MNCs with worldwide networks looking for the cheapest goods and workers being denied their fair share of the benefits; § A Garment Worker — the benefits a permanent worker is entitled to

stem: One of the present debates in India is whether companies should have flexible policies for employment. Based on what you have read in the chapter, summarise the point of view of the employers and workers.
solution:
| Employers' point of view | Workers' point of view |
|---|---|
| Flexibility lets them hire workers only for short periods, when there is intense pressure of work, so they need not pay workers for the whole year. | It makes jobs insecure; when a factory closes a worker may search for months and then get only temporary work far from home. |
| It reduces the cost of labour, which is the only cost they can cut once the cost of raw materials is fixed. | It takes away the benefits of a permanent worker — health insurance, provident fund and overtime at a double rate. |
| Lower costs let them quote the cheapest price and win the large orders placed by foreign MNCs. | Wages fall sharply — Sushila earns less than half of what she earned as a permanent worker, and a day off from work means no wage. |
| Flexibility attracts foreign investment, and foreign companies are demanding still more of it. | Workers must put in very long hours and night shifts and are forced to work overtime to make both ends meet, and are denied their fair share of the benefits of globalisation. |
groundedIn: § Steps to Attract Foreign Investment — the government allowing companies to hire workers ‘flexibly’ for short periods so as to reduce the cost of labour, and foreign companies demanding still more flexibility in the labour laws; § Competition and Uncertain Employment — exporters cutting labour costs, workers working long hours and night shifts, and workers being denied their fair share of the benefits; § A Garment Worker — Sushila's loss of her permanent status, her benefits and half her earnings
